how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation or runbook confirms that unsigned or self-signed certificates are rejected by the server, and new node onboarding requires CA-signed certs.

option_description: Defines how rigorously the configuration server validates host identity tokens — such as bootstrap tokens, API keys, or join tokens — before issuing configuration. 'full' means cryptographic signature verification plus expiry and revocation checks; 'partial' means only some checks are performed (e.g., signature but no revocation); 'none' means tokens are accepted without validation.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'weak_host_identity_verification_by_server' fires when host_token_validation_mode is 'partial' or 'none'. Partial or absent token validation allows revoked, expired, or forged tokens to successfully authenticate, enabling rogue hosts to obtain configurations and supporting T1649 (Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates) attacks. Only 'full' validation mode closes this gap.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Ansible Tower/AWX, inspect the settings for token validation including expiry enforcement and revocation checking.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -Ei 'token|jwt|expiry|revocation|oauth' /etc/tower/settings.py /etc/tower/conf.d/*.py 2>/dev/null ; awx-manage shell -c 'from django.conf import settings; print(settings.ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_SECONDS)' 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Short token expiry (e.g., 31536000 seconds or less) and revocation list in use indicates at least partial validation. Full validation requires all three checks.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Ansible AWX/Tower, navigate to the OAuth2 Application settings to review token scope, expiry, and revocation policies.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWX/Tower Web UI → Settings → Miscellaneous Authentication → OAuth2 Token Expiration; verify expiry is set and revocation is enforced.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Token expiry value is non-zero and token revocation is enabled for terminated sessions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the configuration server API to test token validation behavior by submitting an expired or malformed token and observing whether it is rejected.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H 'Authorization: Bearer EXPIREDTOKEN123' https://<config-server>:8443/api/v1/nodes && echo 'FAIL: token accepted' || echo 'PASS: token rejected'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: HTTP 401 Unauthorized response confirms token validation is active. HTTP 200 indicates 'none' mode.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For SaltStack with token-based auth, review the eauth and token TTL configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'token_expire: 43200' (12 hours) with eauth configured indicates partial validation. Full validation requires revocation checking via external auth provider.

option_description: Controls whether the configuration server automatically signs or accepts certificate signing requests (CSRs) or node registration requests without requiring manual operator review and approval. When enabled, any host that can reach the server can register itself and begin receiving configurations.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'weak_host_identity_verification_by_server' fires when auto_sign_enabled is true. Auto-signing eliminates the human verification step in node enrollment, allowing any attacker who can reach the configuration server to register a rogue host and receive configuration payloads — potentially including credentials or sensitive infrastructure details. This directly enables T1649 and T1608.003 attacks.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Puppet, check autosign.conf and the autosign setting in puppet.conf. A wildcard entry or 'autosign = true' is a critical finding.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'autosign = false' or no autosign.conf (file absent) is secure. 'autosign = true' or a wildcard '*' in autosign.conf is a critical finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For SaltStack, check the auto_accept setting in the master configuration which controls automatic minion key acceptance.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'auto_accept: False' is secure. 'auto_accept: True' or 'open_mode: True' means auto-signing is active — a critical finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Puppet, list currently pending and signed certificate requests to assess whether any wildcard auto-sign pattern is active.
how_to_obtain.command: puppetserver ca list --all 2>/dev/null ; puppet cert list --all 2>/dev/null | grep -v '+ '
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Pending requests that have not been auto-signed suggest auto-signing is disabled. Immediate signing of all requests indicates it is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Chef, check the Chef Infra Server policy for auto-sign behavior and new node validation requirements.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Default Chef behavior requires explicit node registration with a validator key. Absence of restrictions on new client creation is a finding.

option_description: Indicates whether the deployment pipeline or configuration management system has an explicit rollback capability that can revert managed hosts to a previously known-good configuration or deployment revision when a failure or health check violation occurs.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'no_rollback_capability_for_failed_deployments' fires when rollback_mechanism_configured is false. Without rollback, a misconfigured or malicious deployment that disables security controls (firewalls, EDR agents, audit daemons) cannot be rapidly reversed, extending the exposure window. This exacerbates T1072 (Software Deployment Tools) attacks and T1499.004 (Application or System Exploitation) by leaving systems in a broken or compromised state indefinitely.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Kubernetes deployments, verify a rollback strategy exists by inspecting Deployment or Argo CD Application manifests for rollback annotations or strategies.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get deployments -A -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, revisionHistoryLimit: .spec.revisionHistoryLimit, strategy: .spec.strategy}' 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'revisionHistoryLimit' greater than 0 and a defined strategy indicates rollback is possible. Limit of 0 means no rollback target exists.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Helm-managed deployments, check whether rollback hooks or max-history settings are configured.
how_to_obtain.command: helm history <release-name> -n <namespace> 2>/dev/null ; helm get values <release-name> -n <namespace> 2>/dev/null | grep -i rollback ; cat helmfile.yaml 2>/dev/null | grep -i rollback
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Multiple revision entries in helm history indicate rollback targets exist. 'helm rollback' should be executable without error.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Ansible-based deployments, search the playbook repository for rollback plays or tags.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one playbook or role tagged 'rollback' or 'revert' confirms a rollback mechanism is defined.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Spinnaker, Jenkins X, or ArgoCD, review the pipeline definition for a rollback or undo stage.
how_to_obtain.navigation: ArgoCD UI → Application → History and Rollback tab; Spinnaker UI → Pipeline → Edit Pipeline → look for Rollback Cluster or Undo Rollout stage.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A visible rollback or undo stage in the pipeline configuration confirms the mechanism is configured.

option_description: Defines what initiates a rollback when a rollback mechanism is configured: 'automatic' means the system triggers rollback based on health checks, failed readiness probes, or pipeline gate failures without human intervention; 'manual' means an operator must explicitly invoke rollback; 'none' means no trigger exists and rollback cannot be initiated.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'no_rollback_capability_for_failed_deployments' fires when rollback_trigger_type is 'none', even if rollback_mechanism_configured is true — because a mechanism without a trigger is effectively unusable. Manual triggers introduce operator response latency, while automatic triggers minimize the window during which a broken or compromised configuration is active, directly limiting the impact of T1072 (Software Deployment Tools) attacks.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Kubernetes, check Deployment readiness and liveness probe configurations that feed into automatic rollback via rollout status.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get deployment <name> -n <namespace> -o json | jq '{readinessProbe: .spec.template.spec.containers[].readinessProbe, progressDeadlineSeconds: .spec.progressDeadlineSeconds}' 2>/dev/null ; kubectl rollout status deployment/<name> -n <namespace> 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of readinessProbe and a defined progressDeadlineSeconds enables automatic rollback on failed rollouts. Absence indicates manual-only or none.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For ArgoCD, inspect the Application sync policy for automated rollback or self-heal settings.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get application <app-name> -n argocd -o json | jq '.spec.syncPolicy' 2>/dev/null ; cat argocd-application.yaml 2>/dev/null | grep -A10 'syncPolicy'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'selfHeal: true' and 'automated: {}' in syncPolicy indicates automatic remediation/rollback is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Spinnaker, review whether pipeline stages include automated failure conditions that invoke a Rollback Cluster or Undo Rollout stage.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Spinnaker UI → Pipelines → [Pipeline Name] → Edit → Locate Rollback/Undo stage and check 'Trigger on' conditions; Jenkins → Pipeline → View Script for 'post { failure { ... } }' rollback invocations.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A stage with automatic failure trigger conditions set (not requiring manual gate approval) confirms 'automatic' trigger type.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Ansible AWX/Tower, check workflow job template definitions for rollback playbook linkage triggered by failure conditions.
how_to_obtain.command: awx workflow_job_templates list --all -f json 2>/dev/null | python3 -c "import json,sys; wf=json.load(sys.stdin); [print(w['name'], w.get('failure_node')) for w in wf.get('results', [])]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Workflow templates with a 'failure_node' pointing to a rollback playbook indicate automatic triggering on failure.

option_description: Specifies how many previous deployment revisions, snapshots, or artifact versions the deployment system retains. This count determines whether a concrete rollback target exists. A value of 0 means no history is kept, making rollback impossible even if a rollback mechanism is configured.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'no_rollback_capability_for_failed_deployments' fires when rollback_mechanism_configured is true but deployment_history_versions_retained equals 0, because a rollback mechanism without a stored prior revision cannot function. Zero history permanently eliminates rollback capability regardless of pipeline configuration, meaning any malicious or broken deployment becomes irreversible without manual reconstruction — amplifying T1072 and T1499.004 impact.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Kubernetes Deployments, check the revisionHistoryLimit field which controls how many ReplicaSets are retained for rollback.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get deployments -A -o custom-columns='NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,HISTORY_LIMIT:.spec.revisionHistoryLimit' 2>/dev/null ; kubectl get deployment <name> -n <namespace> -o jsonpath='{.spec.revisionHistoryLimit}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A value of 3-10 is typical for retaining enough history. A value of 0 or empty (defaults to 10 in Kubernetes but may be explicitly set to 0) is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Helm, list release history to see how many revisions are retained and check the helm max-history configuration.
how_to_obtain.command: helm history <release-name> -n <namespace> --max 20 2>/dev/null ; helm env | grep HELM_MAX_HISTORY ; grep -Ei 'max.history|historyMax' ~/.helm/repositories.yaml /etc/helm/*.yaml 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Multiple revision entries (e.g., 3 or more) in 'helm history' output confirm history is retained. HELM_MAX_HISTORY=0 means unlimited history is kept (acceptable).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the ArgoCD or Flux API to retrieve the number of retained deployment revisions for managed applications.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get application <app-name> -n argocd -o jsonpath='{.spec.revisionHistoryLimit}' 2>/dev/null ; argocd app history <app-name> --output wide 2>/dev/null | wc -l
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ArgoCD default is 10 revisions. An explicit value of 0 or 1 limits rollback options significantly and should be flagged.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For CI/CD systems like GitLab CI or GitHub Actions with artifact retention, check the pipeline definition for artifact or deployment snapshot retention policies.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Artifact expiry set to at least several days (e.g., '30 days') and multiple deployment snapshots retained confirms adequate history. Immediate expiry or no retention policy is a finding.

option_description: Controls whether sensitive environment variables (API keys, passwords, tokens) are injected into deployment processes via command-line arguments, which exposes them in OS process tables visible to any local user via /proc or ps output.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the 'environment_variable_leakage_in_deployment_context' exposure when env_vars_passed_as_plaintext_args is true AND secrets_manager_integration_used is false, or when plaintext args are used AND shell_history_persistence_disabled is false. Plaintext CLI arguments are readable by any user who can list processes (T1552 Unsecured Credentials, T1552.003 Shell History).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect running deployment processes for secrets passed as CLI arguments using ps or /proc enumeration
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No matches expected in a secure deployment; any output indicates plaintext secrets in process arguments

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review CI/CD pipeline definitions (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins) for hardcoded secret values passed as --extra-vars, -e, or --var flags
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No matches; secrets should reference ${{ secrets.NAME }} or similar vault lookups rather than inline values

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Ansible playbooks and inventory files for vars or extra-vars blocks containing literal secret values
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secrets should reference ansible-vault encrypted strings (!vault |) or lookup('env', 'VAR') rather than plaintext values

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check CI/CD pipeline run logs and deployment audit trails for command invocations that include literal secret values
how_to_obtain.command: journalctl -u jenkins --since '7 days ago' | grep -E '(password|secret|token|api_key)=[^$\{]' | head -50
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries should show masked values (***) or environment variable references, not literal secret strings

typical_values: true (common in legacy pipelines using --extra-vars or -e flags)
false (desired state with secrets manager integration)

option_description: Governs how much detail deployment tools capture in their output logs and CI/CD pipeline artifacts, including whether resolved environment variable values containing secrets appear as plaintext in stored log files.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'environment_variable_leakage_in_deployment_context' when deployment_output_logging_level is 'verbose_with_secrets' AND secrets_manager_integration_used is false. Verbose logs stored in CI/CD artifact storage, S3 buckets, or log aggregators expose credentials to anyone with log read access (T1552 Unsecured Credentials).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Terraform logging environment variables and configuration for log verbosity settings that capture variable values
how_to_obtain.expected_output: TF_LOG should be unset or set to ERROR/WARN; TF_LOG=TRACE or DEBUG captures all variable values including secrets

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Ansible configuration for verbosity level settings and check for -v/-vvv flags in invocation wrappers
how_to_obtain.expected_output: verbosity should be 0 or 1; display_args_to_stdout should be False; no_log should be True on sensitive tasks

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review CI/CD pipeline settings in Jenkins, GitHub Actions, or GitLab for debug logging toggles and check stored build artifacts for secret exposure
how_to_obtain.navigation: Jenkins: Job > Configure > Build Environment > check for 'Print environment variables'; GitHub Actions: Repository > Settings > Actions > Runner debug logging (ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG); GitLab: CI/CD > Settings > Variables > check for CI_DEBUG_TRACE
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Debug/trace logging should be disabled in production pipelines; CI_DEBUG_TRACE and ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG should be false or absent

how_to_obtain.instruction: Scan existing deployment log archives for patterns indicating secret values were captured at verbose logging level
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No log files should contain resolved secret values; only masked (***) or environment variable references

typical_values: verbose_with_secrets (common during debugging, risky if logs persisted)

option_description: Controls whether shell command history recording is suppressed on deployment hosts and CI/CD runner accounts, preventing commands that include secret values from being written to ~/.bash_history or equivalent persistent files on disk.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'environment_variable_leakage_in_deployment_context' when env_vars_passed_as_plaintext_args is true AND shell_history_persistence_disabled is false, because plaintext CLI arguments containing secrets would then persist to history files readable by local users (T1552.003 Shell History).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check HISTFILE, HISTSIZE, and HISTFILESIZE environment variable settings for deployment service accounts
how_to_obtain.command: sudo -u deploy-svc bash -c 'echo HISTFILE=$HISTFILE; echo HISTSIZE=$HISTSIZE; echo HISTFILESIZE=$HISTFILESIZE; echo HISTCONTROL=$HISTCONTROL' 2>/dev/null || grep -E 'HIST' /home/deploy*/.bashrc /home/deploy*/.bash_profile /root/.bashrc 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: HISTFILE should be unset or /dev/null; HISTSIZE=0; HISTFILESIZE=0; or HISTCONTROL=ignorespace:erasedups

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review system-wide shell profile files for history suppression directives applied to deployment accounts
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Should see 'export HISTFILE=/dev/null', 'export HISTSIZE=0', or 'unset HISTFILE' in profile scripts for deployment accounts

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for existing history files on deployment hosts that may contain previously recorded secret-bearing commands
how_to_obtain.expected_output: History files for deployment accounts should not exist, be empty (0 bytes), or be symlinked to /dev/null

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview DevOps team and review runbook documentation to confirm shell history suppression is part of deployment host hardening standard
how_to_obtain.file_path: Deployment host hardening checklist, CIS benchmark implementation records, Ansible hardening playbooks
how_to_obtain.navigation: Review configuration management playbooks for tasks that set HISTFILE=/dev/null or equivalent in deployment account profiles
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Written policy and implemented configuration tasks confirming shell history is disabled for all deployment service accounts

typical_values: false (default on most systems; history enabled unless explicitly disabled)
true (hardened deployment hosts with HISTFILE=/dev/null or HISTSIZE=0)

option_description: Indicates whether the deployment pipeline retrieves sensitive configuration values (credentials, API keys, certificates) at runtime from a dedicated secrets management service such as HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or Azure Key Vault, rather than embedding them in pipeline definitions or environment blocks.
security_impact: The Rego policy uses secrets_manager_integration_used as a mitigating control: both the plaintext args leakage condition and verbose logging leakage condition only fire when NOT input.secrets_manager_integration_used. Without a secrets manager, secrets must reside somewhere in plaintext in the pipeline, making them accessible to anyone with pipeline or config access (T1552 Unsecured Credentials, T1552.001 Credentials In Files).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search deployment pipeline definitions and configuration management code for secrets manager API calls or lookup integrations
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Should find vault_read(), aws_secretsmanager_secret_version data sources, Parameter Store lookups, or equivalent secrets manager integrations

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for Vault agent or AWS credential helper processes running on deployment hosts indicating active secrets manager integration
how_to_obtain.command: ps aux | grep -E '(vault agent|aws-vault|chamber|berglas|secret-manager)' | grep -v grep; systemctl list-units --state=running | grep -E '(vault|secrets)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: vault agent process or equivalent secrets manager daemon should be running; absence suggests no live secrets manager integration

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the CI/CD platform API to verify secrets are stored in the platform's secrets store rather than as plaintext environment variables in pipeline definitions
how_to_obtain.command: gh secret list --repo <org>/<repo> 2>/dev/null || gitlab-ci-lint .gitlab-ci.yml; curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $VAULT_TOKEN' $VAULT_ADDR/v1/sys/mounts | jq 'keys'
how_to_obtain.navigation: GitHub: Repository > Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions; GitLab: Project > Settings > CI/CD > Variables (check 'Masked' and 'Protected' flags); Jenkins: Manage Jenkins > Credentials
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secrets should exist as platform-managed masked/encrypted variables or Vault references, not plaintext values in YAML definitions

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Terraform provider configurations and Ansible vault or lookup plugin usage to confirm secrets manager backends are defined
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Vault provider blocks, aws_secretsmanager data sources, or hashi_vault lookups confirm secrets manager integration is configured

typical_values: false (common in smaller organizations or legacy pipelines)
true (mature DevSecOps environments with Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or Azure Key Vault)

option_description: Controls whether the configuration management tool is configured to guarantee that repeated or interrupted configuration runs always converge to the same defined end state, preventing partial application of configurations that could leave security controls in an inconsistent or weakened condition.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'missing_idempotency_enforcement_allowing_partial_state' when idempotency_enforcement_enabled is false AND either security_critical_resources_managed has entries OR partial_run_detection_enabled is false. Without idempotency, an interrupted run could apply firewall rule deletions but not replacements, or half-apply sudo configurations, leaving systems temporarily or permanently exposed (T1578.005, T1546).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Ansible configuration for any_errors_fatal, max_fail_percentage, and error handling settings that enforce full convergence
how_to_obtain.expected_output: any_errors_fatal: true and max_fail_percentage: 0 indicate idempotency enforcement; ignore_errors: true on security tasks is a risk signal

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Chef and Puppet run configurations for convergence enforcement settings and why-run mode being disabled in production
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E '(chef_client_daemon_options|why.run|noop|no.op|--why-run|enforce_idempotency)' /etc/chef/client.rb /etc/puppetlabs/puppet/puppet.conf 2>/dev/null; puppet config print noop --section agent
how_to_obtain.expected_output: noop should be false in production; Puppet/Chef agents should run in enforcement (not dry-run) mode with convergence verified

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check CI/CD pipeline definitions for deployment stages that include convergence verification steps or rollback-on-failure mechanisms
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Pipeline stages should include post-deployment verification steps; on_failure handlers should trigger rollback or re-run to full convergence

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview configuration management team and review operational runbooks to determine if idempotency testing is part of the change validation process
how_to_obtain.file_path: Change management runbooks, Ansible playbook test suites (Molecule), Puppet/Chef test-kitchen configurations
how_to_obtain.navigation: Review pull request templates for idempotency test requirements; check Molecule test suites for idempotency test stages (--idempotency-check)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Evidence of automated idempotency testing (Molecule idempotency stage, Puppet RSpec, Test Kitchen) and documented enforcement policy

typical_values: false (default in many Ansible environments without explicit any_errors_fatal)
true (mature CM environments with convergence testing and error enforcement)

option_description: Enumerates the categories of security-sensitive system resources (firewall rules, file permissions, sudoers, SSH keys, SELinux/AppArmor policies, audit rules) that are actively managed by the configuration management tool, indicating which security controls are at risk of partial state if idempotency is not enforced.
security_impact: The Rego policy uses this array as a risk amplifier for 'missing_idempotency_enforcement_allowing_partial_state': when count(security_critical_resources_managed) > 0 AND idempotency_enforcement_enabled is false, the exposure fires. The more critical resource types managed, the broader the potential security control failure from a partial or interrupted configuration run.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Scan Ansible playbooks and roles for modules that manage security-critical resource categories
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of files containing security-critical resource management; each module type maps to a resource category (e.g., iptables -> firewall_rules, file with mode -> file_permissions)

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Puppet manifests and modules for defined resources managing security-critical types
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Puppet .pp files referencing Firewall, Sudo, Ssh_authorized_key, File with mode/owner attributes, or SELinux resources indicate managed security-critical types

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Terraform and Salt state files for security infrastructure resource definitions
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Security group resources, IAM policy resources, or Salt states managing firewall/sudo/SSH indicate fleet-wide security resource management scope

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the CM tool's resource inventory or run a dry-run/check mode to enumerate all resource types currently under management
how_to_obtain.command: ansible-playbook site.yml --list-tasks 2>/dev/null | grep -E '(iptables|firewall|sudo|ssh|selinux|apparmor|audit|pam|acl|chmod|chown)'; puppet resource --types 2>/dev/null | grep -E '(firewall|sudo|ssh_auth)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Task listing should enumerate security-relevant modules; cross-reference against known critical types: firewall_rules, file_permissions, sudoers, ssh_keys, selinux_policy, audit_rules, pam_config

typical_values: [] (CM tool not managing security-critical resources, potentially risky gap)

option_description: Controls whether the configuration management system actively monitors deployment runs for incomplete or interrupted execution, triggering alerts or automated remediation when a run exits before applying all defined configurations, preventing silent partial states that could leave security controls misconfigured.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'missing_idempotency_enforcement_allowing_partial_state' when idempotency_enforcement_enabled is false AND partial_run_detection_enabled is false. Without either idempotency or partial run detection, a failed run that half-applies firewall rules or sudo configurations would go undetected, creating a security gap window of unknown duration (T1578.005, T1546).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check CI/CD pipeline definitions for post-deployment compliance validation gates and failure notification steps
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Pipeline stages should include post-deployment verification steps (InSpec, Serverspec, or custom health checks) that fail the pipeline if configurations are incomplete

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Puppet, Chef, or Ansible reporting and callback configurations for run status monitoring and alerting
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Ansible should have profile_tasks or mail/slack callbacks enabled; Puppet should have reports = puppetdb,log configured; Chef should have report handlers defined

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the configuration management server API for recent run reports and verify failed or partial runs generate alerts
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'X-Authentication: $PUPPET_TOKEN' https://puppet-server:8081/pdb/query/v4/reports?query='["=","status","failed"]' | jq 'length'; knife runs list --run-id $(knife runs list | head -1 | awk '{print $1}') 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.navigation: Puppet Enterprise: Reports > Filter by status=Failed; Chef Automate: Infrastructure > Runs > filter Failed; Ansible Tower/AWX: Jobs > filter Failed
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Failed runs should appear in the management console; alerting integrations should generate tickets or notifications when status != successful

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review deployment logs and monitoring system for evidence that partial run failures are being captured and acted upon
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Failed runs should be logged with non-zero exit codes; corresponding alerts in monitoring systems (PagerDuty, Slack, email) should be traceable to these log events

typical_values: false (common default; many pipelines only check final exit code without post-run validation)
true (mature pipelines with InSpec compliance gates, run report monitoring, and alerting integrations)
